newsitem.title: USA: DIVING-U.S. QUALIFIES FOUR DIVERS BUT CHINA STILL DOMINATES.
newsitem.headline: DIVING-U.S. QUALIFIES FOUR DIVERS BUT CHINA STILL DOMINATES.

text.p: For the first time since 1993, the United States qualified four divers for the championship final of a major international meet Thursday at the FINA/USA Diving Grand Prix.
But in what seemed like a rerun of every major meet since the late 1980s, Chinese still dominated the final, finishing first and second.

Zhou Yi Lin, with 434.16 points, and Yu Zhuo Cheng (426.42) took the top two spots while Californian Troy Dumais finished third (418.20). It was the smallest point differential Dumais has achieved against the Chinese.
Zhou scored 85.68 points on an inward 2 1/2 somersault. The dive has a 3.4 degree of difficulty and in Thursday's final was attempted only by the Chinese.
P.J. Bogart, Chris Devine, and Bryan Gillooly were the other American finalists.
"We are getting closer," said Dumais, at 17 the youngest American in the final. But he conceded the United States is still way below the level it once held as a world power in the sport.

"To tell you the truth I couldn't tell you when in the United States we will be able to take over again for a long time," Dumais said. "We don't have the training time they do. They train nine hours a day. We have other things to do. We have a life."
The meet was the first major international meet since the Olympic Games in Atlanta, where China won five medals -- three gold, one silver and one bronze medal.
"Every one of their dives impressed me," Dumais said. "It was just trying to follow them was the thing. I wasn't thinking 'oh my gosh, how am I going to beat that?' I just tried to flow with it."
The 1-meter springboard is not an Olympic event. Zhou, 23, ranked sixth last year, is now his country's best 1-meter diver. He goes to school three half-days a week. The rest of the time he trains.

The incentives are great, according to five-time Chinese Olympian Kongzheng Li, now a U.S. national team coach and University of Minnesota coach. Gold medals are worth $30,000 to $40,000, a new house and a possible coaching position in a sports academy after retirement from diving.
China's mass production of divers at young ages is looked down upon by coaches and divers around the world, but China has dominated the sport since Greg Louganis retired in 1988.

"We (the United States) close the gap little by little, but not enough to win," Kongzheng said. "If we had the time, the money, the incentives and the support, we would improve. But we would never adapt to their system. It is too hard on divers."

Despite the dismissal of national team coach Xu Yiming and a shakeup in China's national team programme, its divers still jump higher and spin faster than any other country's while attempting the most difficult dives.
Men's 1-meter springboard final
1. Zhou Yi Lin (China) 434.16
2. Yu Zhuo Cheng (China) 426.42
3. Troy Dumais (U.S.) 418.20
4. P.J. Bogart (U.S.) 371.94
5. Chris Devine (U.S.) 367.02
6. Bryan Gillooly (U.S.) 315.39
